headings.title: Introduction to Body Fluids and Compartments
headings.content: Body fluids are essential for maintaining homeostasis, transporting nutrients, and removing waste products in the human body. Total body water (TBW) constitutes a significant percentage of body weight, typically around 60% in adult males and slightly less in adult females, varying with age, gender, and adipose tissue content. Fat tissue contains very little water, meaning obese individuals have a lower percentage of total body water compared to lean individuals. For nursing students in Nigeria, understanding how body fluids are partitioned is foundational to recognizing fluid shifts and managing patient hydration accurately. Fluid is primarily divided into two main compartments: the intracellular fluid (ICF) compartment and the extracellular fluid (ECF) compartment. Intracellular fluid is located within the cells and accounts for roughly two-thirds (about 40% of body weight) of the total body water, serving as the primary site for metabolic processes. Conversely, extracellular fluid comprises the remaining one-third of total body water and surrounds the cells. The ECF is further subdivided into distinct sub-compartments: the intravascular fluid (plasma, found within blood vessels), the interstitial fluid (surrounding tissue cells), and transcellular fluid (such as cerebrospinal, synovial, peritoneal, and pleural fluids). Movement and balance between these compartments are strictly regulated to maintain cellular integrity and stable systemic blood pressure. Disruptions in these compartments can lead to critical clinical states, such as edema or cellular dehydration, which require prompt nursing intervention and continuous assessment.

headings.title: Electrolyte Composition of Body Fluids
headings.content: Electrolytes are electrically charged minerals dissolved in body fluids that play a vital role in nerve conduction, muscle contraction, and maintaining acid-base balance and osmotic pressure. The composition of electrolytes varies markedly between the intracellular fluid (ICF) and extracellular fluid (ECF) compartments, creating crucial chemical gradients. In the ECF, sodium (Na+) is the predominant cation, responsible for maintaining extracellular ososmotic pressure and fluid balance, while chloride (Cl-) and bicarbonate (HCO3-) are the major anions. Conversely, the ICF has a high concentration of potassium (K+) as the primary cation, along with magnesium (Mg2+) and phosphate (HPO42-). Protein anions are also heavily concentrated inside the cells. This distinct distribution is maintained actively by cellular mechanisms, most notably the sodium-potassium adenosine triphosphatase (Na+/K+ ATPase) pump, which expels three sodium ions out of the cell for every two potassium ions it pumps in. For nursing students, memorizing these normal distributions is clinically critical. Alterations in these electrolyte levels can lead to life-threatening conditions. For instance, hyperkalemia (high serum potassium) or hypokalemia (low serum potassium) can severely disrupt cardiac electrical conduction, leading to fatal arrhythmias. Similarly, abnormalities in sodium levels can cause neurological symptoms ranging from confusion to seizures. Understanding electrolyte composition allows nurses to accurately interpret laboratory values and administer corrective intravenous solutions safely.

headings.title: Mechanisms of Fluid Movement Across Membranes
headings.content: The movement of water and dissolved solutes across semipermeable membranes between body fluid compartments is governed by several core physiological and physical principles. Osmosis is the passive movement of water molecules across a semipermeable membrane from an area of lower solute concentration to an area of higher solute concentration, driven by osmotic pressure. Tonicity describes how an extracellular solution can change the volume of a cell by altering its water content through osmosis. Isotonic solutions have the same effective osmolality as blood plasma, causing no net fluid shift, whereas hypotonic solutions cause water to move into cells, potentially leading to cellular swelling and lysis. Hypertonic solutions draw water out of cells into the ECF, causing cellular shrinkage. Diffusion involves the passive movement of solutes (such as electrolytes and gases like oxygen and carbon dioxide) from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration until equilibrium is reached. Active transport requires metabolic energy (ATP) to move solutes against their concentration gradient, as seen with the sodium-potassium pump. Finally, filtration is the movement of water and solutes through a membrane driven by hydrostatic pressure, which is the pressure exerted by fluid against a container wall or capillary membrane, such as blood pressure pushing fluid out of the capillary bed. Understanding these mechanisms helps nurses anticipate how intravenous fluids, diuretics, and pathological states will impact a patient's fluid distribution.

headings.title: Hormonal Regulation of Fluid and Electrolyte Balance
headings.content: Fluid and electrolyte balance in the human body is tightly regulated by intricate hormonal and neuroendocrine feedback loops that respond to changes in blood volume, blood pressure, and plasma osmolality. Antidiuretic hormone (ADH), also known as vasopressin, is synthesized in the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary gland. ADH release is stimulated by an increase in plasma osmolality or a significant decrease in blood volume. It acts on the renal collecting ducts to increase water reabsorption, concentrating the urine and returning water to the circulation, thereby lowering serum osmolality. The Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS) is another vital hormonal cascade activated when renal perfusion or blood pressure drops. Renin is released by the kidneys, converting angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, which is subsequently converted to angiotensin II by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE). Angiotensin II is a powerful vasoconstrictor and stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone. Aldosterone promotes the renal retention of sodium and water while enhancing the excretion of potassium, effectively expanding extracellular fluid volume and raising blood pressure. Additionally, atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) is released by atrial myocardial cells in response to excessive stretching caused by hypervolemia. ANP promotes sodium and water excretion by the kidneys, acting as a natural antagonist to the RAAS to lower blood volume. For nursing students, recognizing how these hormones operate is essential for interpreting clinical signs like oliguria, edema, and electrolyte disturbances.

headings.title: Daily Fluid Intake and Output Pathways
headings.content: To maintain fluid homeostasis, healthy individuals must maintain a dynamic equilibrium where daily fluid intake approximately equals daily fluid output. Fluid intake is regulated primarily through the thirst mechanism, controlled by osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus that detect increases in plasma osmolality or decreases in blood volume. Oral fluid consumption (water, beverages, and water contained in solid foods) constitutes the primary source of exogenous intake, complemented by a small amount of water produced metabolically through cellular respiration. Fluid output occurs through multiple pathways, both sensible and insensible. Sensible fluid loss can be measured directly, which includes urine output (the major route of fluid loss), gastrointestinal loss via feces, and wound drainage. Insensible fluid loss is continuous and unmeasurable by standard clinical means, occurring through evaporation from the skin (perspiration) and the respiratory tract via expired air. Under normal ambient conditions, an adult excretes roughly 1,500 mL of urine daily, with insensible losses accounting for about 800 to 1,000 mL divided between skin and lungs. For nurses, monitoring intake and output (I&O) charts is a core responsibility. In tropical environments like Nigeria, high ambient temperatures can significantly increase insensible fluid loss through sweating and respiration, requiring adjustments in fluid intake recommendations to prevent dehydration, particularly in vulnerable populations such as infants and the elderly.

headings.title: Pathophysiology of Fluid Imbalances: Dehydration and Overhydration
headings.content: Fluid imbalances occur when the body's compensatory mechanisms fail to maintain equilibrium between intake and output, leading to deficits or excesses in total body water. Dehydration, or fluid volume deficit (FVD), occurs when water loss exceeds water intake. This can result from inadequate fluid ingestion, excessive gastrointestinal losses (vomiting, diarrhea, or nasogastric suction), excessive renal excretion (polyuria from diuretics or diabetes), or profuse sweating (diaphoresis). Clinical manifestations of dehydration include poor skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, sunken eyeballs, tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria, and altered mental status due to cerebral cellular shrinkage. Conversely, overhydration, or fluid volume excess (FVE), occurs when fluid intake or retention exceeds the body's excretory capacity, often resulting from renal failure, heart failure, excessive sodium intake, or rapid administration of intravenous fluids. Overhydration leads to hypervolemia and edema as fluid shifts into the interstitial spaces. Symptoms include peripheral edema, rapid weight gain, jugular venous distension, elevated blood pressure, dyspnea, crackles in the lungs, and pulmonary edema. Nurses play a critical role in identifying these imbalances early, monitoring laboratory values such as hematocrit and serum electrolytes, and implementing appropriate interventions to restore fluid balance safely and effectively.

headings.title: Clinical Assessment and Monitoring of Fluid Status
headings.content: Accurate clinical assessment and ongoing monitoring of a patient's fluid status are essential competencies for professional nurses. A comprehensive evaluation combines subjective data, objective physical examinations, and diagnostic laboratory findings. Daily weight measurement is considered the single most sensitive, reliable, and objective indicator of overall fluid balance changes; an acute gain or loss of 1 kilogram of body weight is roughly equivalent to retaining or losing 1 liter of fluid. Maintaining a meticulous Intake and Output (I&O) record is another fundamental duty, tracking all oral, enteral, and parenteral fluid inputs against all measurable outputs, including urine, emesis, wound drainage, and diarrhea. Physical examination techniques include assessing vital signs (hypotension and tachycardia often indicate deficit, while hypertension and bounding pulses indicate excess), evaluating skin turgor, inspecting mucous membranes, checking for peripheral or sacral edema, assessing jugular venous pressure, and auscultating lung sounds for adventitious breath sounds like crackles, which signal fluid overload in the pulmonary circulation. Laboratory diagnostics provide critical objective data; hematocrit levels often rise during dehydration due to hemoconcentration and fall during overhydration due to hemodilution, while serum electrolyte panels, urine specific gravity, and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) levels help determine the specific nature of the fluid and electrolyte disturbance.
